reference.source: Standard endocrinology and radiology reference texts and adrenal incidentaloma consensus guidance
clinicalPearls: A benign, hormonally inactive adrenal tumour composed of mature adipose tissue admixed with haematopoietic elements, most often found incidentally on imaging
The presence of macroscopic (bulk) fat on CT or MRI is the key diagnostic feature and reliably distinguishes it from most other adrenal masses
Usually asymptomatic, but large lesions can cause flank or abdominal pain, or present acutely with retroperitoneal haemorrhage
Being non-functioning, it does not require the full hormonal excess workup once fat content confirms the diagnosis, though a screening biochemical assessment of an incidentaloma remains prudent
Small, uncomplicated lesions can be managed conservatively with surveillance rather than surgery
Larger tumours (commonly beyond around 6 to 7 cm) carry a higher risk of spontaneous bleeding and may be considered for resection
Can rarely coexist with, or be mimicked by, other fat-containing retroperitoneal lesions such as liposarcoma, which should be considered if imaging is atypical
reference.pathophysiology: Adrenal myelolipoma is a benign tumour formed by metaplastic transformation of adrenal cortical stromal cells into mature fat and functioning haematopoietic (myeloid and erythroid) tissue. It is not derived from steroidogenic cells and therefore does not secrete hormones. The proportion of fat to marrow elements varies, giving the characteristic mixed density on imaging. Growth is generally slow; the main clinical consequence of larger lesions is mechanical, with the friable, vascular tissue prone to spontaneous or trauma-related haemorrhage. An association with chronic ACTH stimulation and some congenital adrenal disorders has been described.
additionalInvestigations: Non-contrast CT demonstrating macroscopic fat with low Hounsfield attenuation within the mass
MRI with chemical-shift and fat-suppression sequences to confirm bulk fat content
Baseline biochemical screen of an adrenal incidentaloma to confirm the lesion is non-functioning
Assessment of lesion size and any interval growth on follow-up imaging
Evaluation for retroperitoneal haemorrhage if the patient presents with acute pain
Consideration of further characterisation when imaging features are atypical for benign fat
redFlags: Acute flank or abdominal pain with a fall in haemoglobin suggesting spontaneous haemorrhage
Rapid interval growth or heterogeneous soft-tissue components raising concern for liposarcoma
Very large lesion causing mass effect on adjacent structures
Atypical imaging that fails to confirm benign macroscopic fat
reference.prognosis: The lesion is benign with an excellent prognosis; most are managed conservatively with imaging surveillance, and surgery, when needed for size or haemorrhage, is generally curative without recurrence.
pitfalls: Subjecting a clearly fat-containing benign lesion to unnecessary extensive hormonal workup or surgery
Mistaking a fat-containing liposarcoma for a benign myelolipoma when imaging is atypical
Underestimating the haemorrhage risk of a large lesion
Confusing an adrenal myelolipoma with an exophytic renal angiomyolipoma
references: Consensus guidance on management of adrenal incidentalomas
